Grass
GRāS
n. (rendering Hebrew chātsīr and deshe', Greek chortos)
From Old English gaers, of the same root as grow and green. The Hebrew chātsīr is the green herbage of the field, and in the Palestinian climate its life is startlingly brief: the spring growth that carpets the hills after the rains is scorched brown within weeks by the east wind. The biblical figure is therefore not a general observation about mortality but a description of something the writers watched happen every year.

Biblical Definition

Grass is Scripture's standing figure for the brevity of man, and it is used with a severity that is meant to be heard. Isaiah is commissioned to preach it as his message, and the commission is given in the form of a question and answer: “The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field” (Isa 40:6). It is not only human weakness that is compared to grass but human goodliness — the beauty, achievement, and strength that men suppose will last. The psalmist says the same with more tenderness, and immediately grounds comfort in the contrast: “As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15), the next verses turning to the mercy of the LORD which is from everlasting to everlasting. Peter quotes Isaiah for the express purpose of setting the perishable against the imperishable: “For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away” (1Pe 1:24) — and the verse following is but the word of the Lord endureth for ever. The doctrine is not despair but proportion. And the Lord Jesus takes the same short-lived grass and makes it an argument for confidence rather than dread: “Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?” (Mat 6:30). God spends real beauty on what lasts a fortnight and is then used for fuel; He will not neglect His children.

Webster 1828 Definition

Herbage; the green covering of the fields, proverbially short-lived under the eastern sun; in Scripture the figure of the brevity of all flesh and of human glory, set against the abiding word of the Lord, and the argument for God's care of His people.

expand to see more

GRASS, n. 1. In common usage, herbage; the plants which constitute the food of cattle and other beasts.

2. In botany, a plant having simple leaves, a stem generally jointed and tubular, and the husk or calyx composed of glumes.

3. The green herbage of the field, which springs quickly and as quickly withers under the eastern sun.

4. In Scripture, a figure of the frailty and short continuance of man and of his glory. All flesh is grass. Isaiah 40.

5. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever. Isaiah 40; 1 Pet. 1.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 40:6 — "The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:"

Psalm 103:15 — "As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth."

1 Peter 1:24 — "For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away:"

Matthew 6:30 — "Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?"

Modern Corruption

Human mortality is either denied outright by a culture that hides death and promises indefinite extension, or made an occasion for despair — both of which miss the use Scripture makes of the figure, which is to fix hope on what does not wither.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is the studied refusal to reckon with mortality: death removed from the home to the institution, age treated as a medical failure rather than a season, and the tacit promise that sufficient technique will indefinitely postpone the withering. Scripture's counsel runs directly against it — so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom — and treats the refusal to number them as folly rather than optimism. The rich fool had many goods laid up for many years and had not counted the one night. To say all flesh is grass is not morbidity; it is accuracy, and accuracy is the beginning of wisdom about how a life should be spent.

The opposite reaction takes the figure and stops there, concluding that if man is grass then nothing he does matters. Neither Isaiah nor Peter stops there. In both places the sentence about grass exists to set up its antithesis: but the word of our God shall stand for ever, and Peter adds, and this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you. The point is not that everything perishes but that one thing does not, and that a man may attach himself to it. The Lord Jesus completes the argument in the gentlest direction of all (Mat 6:30): the God who lavishes beauty on grass destined for the oven is not going to neglect His children, so that the brevity of the flower becomes a reason to stop being anxious rather than a reason to despair.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chātsīr is green herbage or grass, proverbially short-lived; deshe' is tender new growth; 'ēseb is herb or vegetation. Greek chortos is grass, herbage, or fodder.

expand to see more

Hebrew chātsīr (H2682) — grass, green herbage; the figure of frailty in Isa 40:6 and Psa 103:15.

Hebrew deshe' (H1877) — tender grass, the first green growth; let the earth bring forth grass (Gen 1:11).

Hebrew 'ēseb (H6212) — herb, vegetation; the herb of the field which man was sentenced to eat (Gen 3:18).

Greek chortos (G5528) — grass, herbage, fodder; the grass of the field which to day is (Mat 6:30).

Greek anthos (G438) — a flower or blossom; the flower of grass that falleth away (1Pe 1:24), quoting Isaiah.

Usage

"Of the prophet's commissioned message: all flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field (Isa 40:6)."

"Of the contrast with the abiding word: the grass withereth... but the word of the Lord endureth for ever (1Pe 1:24-25)."

"Of the argument from the lesser to the greater: if God so clothe the grass of the field... shall he not much more clothe you (Mat 6:30)."
